title: Criterion-referenceability determines LLM-as-a-judge validity across physics assessment formats
extended_summary:
This paper investigates when large language models can be trusted to mark student work in physics, focusing on the validity of "LLM-as-a-judge" across different assessment formats. The authors ask how well LLM marking aligns with human marking for structured physics questions, short-form essays, and scientific plots, and how prompt conditions such as no rubric, correct solutions, false solutions, and anchored exemplars change marking accuracy and rank-order validity. The central concept introduced is "criterion-referenceability," meaning the extent to which a task can be evaluated through explicit, observable grading features rather than holistic judgment.

The study evaluates multiple frontier models—GPT-5.2, Grok 4.1, Claude Opus 4.5, DeepSeek-V3.2, Gemini Pro 3, and model committees—by re-marking previously human-scored physics responses through API calls under controlled prompting conditions. Data include 771 blind-marked university exam questions, 1,151 structured GCSE, A-Level, and university textbook questions with available solutions, 55 university essay scripts comprising 275 essays, and 1,400 scientific plots from a university laboratory module. The study combines quantitative analyses of error, calibration, and discriminative validity with qualitative analysis of marking disagreements, especially on structured questions.

The population and context are primarily UK physics education settings, especially Durham University undergraduate courses, with an additional secondary-school curriculum question set from OCR GCSE and A-Level physics. However, for the structured-question datasets, the responses being marked were AI-generated rather than authentic student answers; authentic student and AI-authored work were available for the essay and plot datasets. Human markers included question setters, university staff, and experienced module markers. Essays and plots were evaluated in a higher-education context, while the secondary-school component concerned assessment items rather than a live classroom intervention.

The main conclusion is that LLM marking validity depends strongly on task format. For structured questions and code-based scientific plots, LLMs often achieved strong agreement and rank-order validity relative to human markers, especially when official solutions were available. In contrast, essay marking showed poor discriminative validity under all conditions: adding a scheme or anchored exemplars could improve mean scores and reduce absolute error, but did not enable valid differentiation between stronger and weaker essays. The authors conclude that low average error can be misleading, because LLMs may match score distributions without validly discriminating performance, and that AI assessment is most defensible for highly criterion-referenceable tasks rather than holistic writing judgments.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical comparative validation study with clear methods and substantial sample sizes, but it is not a K-12 randomized or quasi-experimental intervention study and much of the data are from university contexts or AI-generated responses rather than authentic secondary student writing. It provides strong measurement evidence but limited causal evidence for educational impact in grades 9-12.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not estimate student learning effects; instead it evaluates assessment validity. Findings suggest potentially meaningful practical value for structured scientific tasks and plot grading, but negative results for essays and the absence of direct K-12 ChatGPT-versus-legacy writing tool comparisons make educational impact unclear overall.

interventions.use_case: LLM-as-a-judge automated marking of physics assessment artifacts, including structured exam responses, short physics essays, and scientific plots, compared against human markers under blind, solution-provided, false-solution, and exemplar-anchored prompting conditions.

finding.finding_summary: For structured physics questions, LLM-based automated marking showed strong agreement with human ranking but only moderate absolute accuracy. On blinded university exam questions (n=771), fractional MAE ranged from 0.202 to 0.250 across models and committee Spearman rho was 0.696; on curriculum structured questions (n=1151), providing correct solutions improved performance (committee rho=0.885, fMAE=0.085), while false solutions worsened absolute accuracy (committee fMAE=0.317) but preserved substantial rank-order validity (committee rho=0.772). For scientific plots (n=1400 plot elements; 100 scripts), discriminative validity was very high (rho>0.84 across models; Gemini rho=0.881) with Gemini MAE=4.2 marks out of 70, within the human-human disagreement range.
finding.measure: Human-AI agreement in physics assessment scoring: fractional mean absolute error, mean absolute error, Spearman rank correlation, quadratic weighted kappa, calibration against human marks
finding.study_size: n=771 exams; n=1151 curriculum structured questions; n=1400 plot elements / 100 scripts
finding.confidence_interval: Structured exams committee rho 95% CI [0.658, 0.731]; curriculum solution committee rho 95% CI [0.872, 0.897]; curriculum false-solution committee rho 95% CI [0.748, 0.794]
finding.std_deviation: Scientific plot pooled human SD=21.8%; pooled AI SD=15.0%

finding.finding_summary: For short-form physics essays, LLM automated marking failed to validly discriminate writing quality relative to aggregated human scores. Across 55 scripts / 275 essays, blind and scheme-only conditions had near-zero rank correlations (committee rho=0.088 blind; rho=-0.044 scheme), and although exemplar anchoring reduced committee MAE to 3.16 marks and shifted the mean near the human mean, discriminative validity remained near zero (committee rho=0.034, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.28]).
finding.measure: Essay scoring agreement with humans using MAE, Spearman rho, QWK, and calibration of holistic marks out of 100
finding.study_size: n=55 scripts; n=275 essays in anchored condition; n=300 pooled marker-level scores for distributional summaries
finding.confidence_interval: Committee blind rho 95% CI [-0.17, 0.34]; committee scheme rho 95% CI [-0.29, 0.21]; committee scheme+anchor rho 95% CI [-0.22, 0.28]
finding.std_deviation: Human essay marks SD=6.1; AI blind SD=11.0; AI scheme SD=9.8; AI scheme+anchor SD=4.3

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions LLM marking as a potential scalable substitute or assistant for human assessment, but the empirical results indicate that operational usefulness depends strongly on task criterion-referenceability. LLMs appear potentially usable for structured physics questions and code-based plots with substantial human-like ranking validity, but are not reliable for holistic essay marking despite lower MAE under anchored prompting, limiting safe workload-reduction claims.
finding.measure: Feasibility of automated marking relative to human scoring accuracy and reliability across task formats
finding.study_size: n=1922 structured questions total; n=55 essay scripts; n=1400 plot elements

finding.finding_summary: The study provides evidence directly relevant to institutional governance of AI assessment: validity depends on task format and prompt/reference conditions, and apparently good distributional agreement can mask invalid ranking. Results support cautious, bounded institutional use of LLM marking for highly criterion-referenceable tasks, while reinforcing policy concerns about sole-use AI marking for open-ended essays.
finding.measure: Assessment validity evidence relevant to governance, fairness, and deployment policy
finding.study_size: n=1922 structured questions total; n=55 essay scripts; n=1400 plot elements
